title: Vasubandhu's Yogacara Text
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of understanding consciousness as the foundation for awakening and living a peaceful life. By grasping the nature of consciousness, we can learn to process emotions wisely, cultivate harmony with the world, and recognize our interconnectedness with all things. This awareness allows us to approach life with clarity, skillfulness, and compassion, ultimately leading to a more awakened and expansive experience of reality.

When Cathy and I were at the Upaya Zen Center for the month of April, and then again when we came home in May, in the Dharma seminar in the Bay Area, we've been studying a wonderful and really important Buddhist text, Vasubandhu's 30 verses.

I have tried to study this text a lot over the years, but I have never been able to understand it because it's pretty technical, and I always found it impossible to grasp in the translations that were available.

So thanks to this work of Ben's, really brilliant work, I'm now able to more or less get something out of this text, and so we've been studying it for the last few months.
Ben's book is called *Inside Vasubandhu's Yogacara, A Practitioner's Guide*, because it is one of the key works of the Yogacara school of Mahayana Buddhist thought.
This school is sometimes called the mind-only school.
Can I press this button?
Yeah.
Hi.
It's called Yogacara because that's the mind-only school, and the reason it's called the mind-only school is because it emphasizes consciousness.
So in a way, the mind-only teachings turn out to be a kind of corrective to the emptiness teachings that we have been talking about.
You may have noticed the emptiness teachings are kind of like a one-trick pony, a one-note melody.
All dharmas are empty.
Emptiness is form.
Form is emptiness.
Emptiness is empty.
It drones on and on and on.
If you read text after text after text, it's droning on and on, saying the same thing.
So there's nothing to anything but talk.
Studying the emptiness teachings could make you a little crazy.
And it could certainly make you wonder why you ought to bother with trying to do something, since nothing is the result of anything and everything.
That would be a misunderstanding of the teachings, but it is a not unlikely misunderstanding.

If you were to really follow these teachings and think about them deeply, you would be drawn swiftly to the conclusion that there's only one thing to do in practice, and that is to realize the empty nature of all dharmas.
I mean, what else would there be?
And it's not a very big step from there to the spirit of the early Zen teachings and teachers.
Sudden awakening.
Just see through everything and you will be brought instantly to peace.
And it's true, we do need to deeply and radically reorient our lives.
As I say, the appearance of dharma to be nice and rational is a little deceptive.
It's actually more radical than it looks or seems to most of us.
Practice cannot be just, let's make things better for me.
It can't be that, because in the end that won't work.
If it would work, it would be fine, but in the end it really won't serve.
So yes, we do need to awaken, and we do need to wake up in this dream life.
You don't wake up little by little by accumulating wisdom and insight and more credentials.
That's not how you wake up.
You wake up all of a sudden.
Or in fact, you don't do it at all, it just happens.
So you have the classic Zen practice: students sweating and laboring over their meditation year after year after year, trying to get suddenly awakened.
In the meantime, however, life is going on.
We have problems, serious problems, and we have to live in this world the way it is.
We probably can't drop everything and rush off to a monastery for decades.
And it turns out that the problem of living in this world isn't so much the world, and all the troublesome people in it and all the screwed up institutions.
It turns out that's not really so much our problem.
Mostly the problem of the world is the problem of our own minds.
Because of course, the world only appears because of our minds, right?
If we didn't have a mind, the world would not appear to us at all.
The world appears to us as it appears to us.
We feel about the world the way we feel about it, and we act in it as we do, because of the condition of our minds.
So on a very practical, down to earth level, if we want to survive the world, we better train our minds.
Because the world is simply going to go on being what it is, you know?
It's going to go on that way.
It's always going to be what it is.
It's not going to be something else.
Our minds will make it into a hell.
Or not.
It's our minds, our faulty visions, our inability to understand and wisely process our own emotions, deepest feelings and thoughts.
That's what makes the world terrible, or potentially beautiful for us.
I'm sure many of you have had the experience, or if you haven't had it, you've certainly heard many stories, about something really terrible happening.
The last thing in the world one would ever have wanted to happen, and it happens.
But it turns out to be beautiful, and wonderful.
A death that turned out to provide a time of tremendous healing and appreciation.
A forced job loss that turned out to be a gift, a blessing in disguise.
A bitter divorce that led to a new and more awake life, and possibly even an intimate relationship.
Of course, there are many tragic and terrible deaths that leave behind them a lifetime of bitterness.
There are lots of job losses and divorces that destroy our lives.
It depends on the mind, on how you see and react to what happens.

So the Yogacara scholars realized that although all dharmas really are empty, and although realizing this is essential, and is in the end what we need to do to address life's suffering, in the meantime it would be very important to be able to work out things in our minds.
To be able to understand our mind enough so that we can know how to live in a good way, without hurting ourselves, without hurting others.

So the Yogacara scholars were interested in studying and truly understanding consciousness, so that we could access it well enough to be able to shape our emotions and conduct, so that we could live in this world without harm.
That's the intention and the burden of this text, of Vasubandhu's Yogacara text, the 30 verses.
He's painting a big picture, a big picture explanation of the mind and how to practice with it.
As I say, we've been talking about this for several months, so I'm not going to attempt, even if I had several talks, I would not want to attempt to summarize all the things that we've been saying.
The text is a bit intricate and there's too much stuff about it, but the talks are on the Everyday Zen website if you're interested.
Ben's book is readily available and I would really recommend that you read it if you're interested in these teachings.
But for now I want to bring up a few important ideas in the text that we can appreciate without going into the whole thing.
The opening verse, the first of the 30 verses, says:
*Everything conceived as self or others occurs in the transformation of consciousness.*
Self or other refers to the only two things that exist as far as we are concerned.
There's only two things, right, that exist.
Me and everything else.
Two things.
And of those two things, the me part is really the important part.
The rest of it, okay, but me is very important.
So those are the two things that exist.
But no, he's saying, no, actually self and world are nothing more than transformations of consciousness.
They don't really exist as we project them to exist.
Reality, real reality, material reality, spiritual reality, psychological reality, social reality: all of this is just the transformation of consciousness.
Being itself is the flowing, the out rolling, the ongoing whisper of consciousness.
Which is why the school is called the mind-only school, although that's a bit misleading.
So that's the biggest picture.
And now Vasubandhu defines eight different consciousnesses as he tries to show us how this transformation of consciousness unfolds.
So he draws a map of eight consciousnesses.
One wonderful thing about Buddhist thought throughout the ages is that all Buddhist thinkers accept a certain basic format for thinking.
My impression is that in Western philosophy everybody always starts all over again, so understanding one philosopher doesn't much help you to understand another one.
But in Buddhist thought everybody's sort of operating on the same manual, just making different innovations and changes.
Vasubandhu does the same.
But he does make two historical innovations that I want to tell you about, in his description of the seventh and the eighth consciousnesses.
So the eighth consciousness, the biggest one of all, he names Alaya Vijnana.

The word Vijnana means consciousness, and it comes from a root word meaning to cut, in the sense of separating, discriminating one thing from another, as we were talking about yesterday in relation to words and language.
And Alaya means something like storehouse.
So Alaya Vijnana is storehouse consciousness: the boundless, spacious consciousness in which are stored all the seeds from the past that produce the sprouting growth of today.
As we've been talking, in every moment, in any moment, anything can happen.
Wonderful things could happen.
Terrible things could happen.
We might be wise, we might be quite foolish.
What will arise out of the Alaya Vijnana in this moment depends on our present action, which will activate this or that good or bad seed.
The seeds are already there.
Past deeds, our own and everyone else's, we can't help it.
So all these seeds, like every moment of our life, are given.
And now the question is, what will we do in this given situation?
How will we understand and behave in this given moment?

So in describing Alaya Vijnana, Vasubandhu wants us to understand how big our minds are and how deep they run, and how absolutely important it is, not only for ourselves, but for the whole world, that we know how to think and act skillfully.
How to be skillfully with our emotions.
As the text unfolds, Vasubandhu gives lots of details about this.
And for us in Zen practice, it's actually pretty simple.
We follow precepts.
We try to understand the difference between harmful and beneficial thoughts, words and deeds.
We pay attention to the effects of our thoughts and our behaviors on our life.
Doing a lot of zazen helps, because it makes it more and more possible for us to pay attention without too much distortion.
Then eventually we can begin to see the patterns, how consciousness works to make of our lives a heaven or a hell.
Consciousness is not one thing and the body another thing.
Body and mind are both consciousness.
Both body and mind are a transformation of consciousness.
So paying attention to the body, establishing an intimate relationship with body and mind as one continuous phenomenon, is the important training that we're doing in zazen.
That's why we keep on coming back to the cushion for a lifetime.
We don't like to end the course after one year or two years or three years.

We keep on coming back to the cushion for a lifetime, because there is no end to tuning the body to the mind, and tuning the mind to the body, and tuning the heart to the body to the mind, as we go through the many moments of our lives.
Vasubandhu's second great innovation is the conception of the seventh consciousness, which he calls manas, or mind literally, but it's usually meant as specifically self-consciousness.
He's the first Buddhist scholar to posit the self-consciousness, because as you know, Buddha famously, and maybe for us quite oddly, taught that there is no self, which is puzzling in a way.
But Vasubandhu says, well, there is self-consciousness, which seems to contradict Buddhist teaching, but it doesn't.
Self-consciousness is just a transformation of consciousness, an apparent occurrence, not an actual entity or state.
So it doesn't really contradict, but it's definitely a different way of putting it.
That's where in Zen the sayings about true self and original self come from.
Because Vasubandhu wants us to know that we don't need to ponder and wonder about our self.
Do we have a self or not?
Should we have a self or not?
Do we need a better self?
Can't we get a better self somehow?
No, he's saying the development of self is a natural transformation of consciousness.
That's what consciousness will do.
It will develop as it rolls on, self and other, subject and object.
This is a painful but necessary development.
In other words, you are you for a reason.
It's not a mistake.
There is a reason for all of your foibles and mistakes and character flaws.
They are really important.
Don't make yourself into an object to be analyzed and judged, pushed, poked, prodded and improved.
The purpose of self, Vasubandhu implies as this text rolls on and you think about it.
The purpose of self is to give us exactly the right kind of suffering, the kind that we need so that we can learn how to love and appreciate everybody else, because they're exactly like us.
The reason that I am me is so that I can see and feel and understand that I am you, and you are me.
Without my being there is no you.
And my love and compassion for you is my awakening.
That's why I need the painful self.
Ben's book has a wonderful little epilogue just a few pages long, because he's really speaking as a person who practices Zen with regular people.
He wants the text to be useful to us.
So in his epilogue he outlines four practices that are implied in this text.
The first practice he mentions, he calls developing awareness of the power of Alaya Vijnana, the eighth consciousness, the storehouse consciousness.
And to me I think of it as the practice of awesomeness.
Through Zazen and through appreciation of the teachings over time, we will little by little begin to recognize literally how awesome and vast our seemingly little lives actually are.
I appear to be speaking, but it's not really me who's speaking.
It's my mother and father talking through my voice.
It's all my relatives through many, many generations talking.
It's all the sages of our tradition and every other tradition talking.
It's all the suffering people of the world and all the animals and plants talking.
It's the same when you're talking: every word that comes out of your mouth has all of that in it.
Paying attention to the arising of consciousness moment by moment, we will see how immense, mysterious and surpassingly weird it is.
Sometimes we feel it as an aura around perception itself.
Sometimes we sense it in the vividness of a memory.
And we are amazed again and again by our being here at all and by the world being here at all.
Even our stupid thoughts and our ridiculous skirmishes, vast and wide.
And Zazen, especially sesshin and Zazen, certainly helps us to feel this way.
And when we do feel this way, it gives us a whole lot more respect for ourselves and everyone else who is just like us.
We're going to listen more and notice that everyone is always telling us the truth.
Even when they're lying, they're telling us the truth.
We're going to see more.
We're going to feel much, much more.
Dogen writes:
*Buddhas invariably practice complete, awesome presence.
Thus, they are active Buddhas.
Understand that the awesome presence of the entire universe, the awesome presence of the entire earth, as revealed by Buddhas and ancestors, is the hidden, inclusive world.*
The second practice Ben mentions is mindfulness.
Just paying attention.
Especially being aware of body and breath, which is the first foundation of mindfulness.
But also, of course, being aware of thoughts, feelings, afflictive and beneficial states of mind.
Eventually, through practicing like that, becoming aware of the great patterns of suffering and liberation that exist in all of us.
I have a little trouble with the word mindfulness itself, because it sounds like something we're going to do and get better at.
I would rather say mindlessness.
Throw away your mind.
Let go of doing and fixing and grabbing hold of everything with your mind.
Relax.
Be present.
Maybe that's better instead of mindfulness.
Presence.
I like presence better.
Or maybe generous presence.
One of the words that's usually translated with the English word mindfulness is smrty, which has the sense of memory or remembering.
And that's good, because practice, I feel, is actually quite easy.
It isn't really as easy as falling off a log, but pretty much it's like that.
You just fall off a log and you're practicing.
The hard part is remembering to practice.
We get so wrapped up in our habitual self-obsession, which we take completely for granted, that we literally forget to practice almost all the time.
And we have to keep on reminding ourselves.
So mindfulness is forgetting and remembering.
It has to do really with commitment, with recognizing the importance of our lives and what we need to do with them.
The third practice Ben mentions is the practice of awareness of the dependent nature of things.
And this is a very famous one.
Thanks to Thich Nhat Hanh, we all know about this and we really love this practice.
Noticing and appreciating how everything all the time is always connected.
And we know it.
Without the support of others, we're not here.
None of us are here.
As much as people complain about the world and how rotten and violent it is, the truth is the human world is very, very kind.
Thanks to others, we all had breakfast this morning and every morning.
Others grow and process our food.
They deliver it to stores or farmers markets where other people are there to offer it to us.
And we cook it on stoves that other people have designed and manufactured and shipped, in homes that other people built, that we got to by driving our car to go home.
A car that somebody else designed and built.
Many people over many, many years figured out how to make such things.
Driving over roads other people built, financed by tax dollars that we all pooled, administered by governments to make the roads viable.
Human beings are very kind.
We depend on them every day and through their kindness we manage to have really beautiful lives.
I'm so grateful for washing machines.
Not long ago they didn't have them.
People would spend hours and hours and hours a day washing clothes, whacking with sticks and stuff.
Hard work.
Thank you everybody for doing that.
But it's not just human beings whose kindness we depend on.
The Earth is so incredibly kind, so enduring.
All the crappy things we do to the Earth.
The Buddhist sutras often mention this.
You can pee on the Earth and crap on the Earth.
The Earth does not bind.
It says that in the sutras.
Even now we're putting a lot worse bad debris on the Earth than a little poop.
And the Earth is saying, that's okay.
We're the victims, we and other species.
The Earth goes on.
The Earth is so kind.
Air, sky, trees, ocean.
How long would we live without the Earth?
A minute maybe.
We are independent.
Everything is interdependent.
We can't exist without others.
We can't exist without our context.
To open our eyes and notice this and make it an active understanding is a practice.
And that practice is always right there in front of us when we look at anything.
But we forget about it.
All the talk, talk, talk, talk, talk inside our minds and in our world never mentions this.
You can read the entire, I don't know how many thousands of words of the New York Times.
Does anybody read the entire New York Times on any given day?
We take it through a whole day.
You won't find a single word about the interdependent nature of all phenomena and the kindness of others.
You won't find a word about that.
No wonder we forget it.
That's why we have to intentionally remember it.
That's why we need each other.
That's the job of sanghas, right?
That's why we come together in sangha, because we remind each other of this.
We remind each other to notice love and to practice love.
Realizing that we owe our lives to others literally, we know we have to take care of others, of everyone, in every way, in any way that we can.
And no matter how much we do for others, we will never even begin to repay the debt we owe them.
So this is good news.
We can just relax knowing that we are 100% guaranteed to fail to live up to our bodhisattva commitment.
We know this to begin with.
There's no way we can do what must be done.
And that is why bodhisattvas are always glorious failures.
Bodhisattva's success and satisfaction in completing the job is far too limited a framework in which to live.
Only absolute and glorious total failure is a big enough space for bodhisattvas to play.
The fourth and last practice mentioned by Ben is, guess what, zazen.
Zazen, non-dual meditation, which is what zazen technically is called.
Non-dual meditation.
Zazen is brilliant.
I am so impressed by zazen.
I am.
More and more all the time.
I never get tired of it.
It's so impressive to me.
The fourth and last practice.
So easy to do.
Anybody can do zazen.
And so peaceful, so nice.
And so profound.
Nowadays, people refer to it as meditation, but it is not meditation.
Dogen specifically says it's not meditation.
What is it?
As he writes in Fukazazegi, as we maybe chant it or will chant:
*[unclear: "I am a gate"] of repose and bliss.
It is the practice realization.*
Oh, two opposite words in one.
*It is the practice realization.
A complete enlightenment.*
In zazen, he goes on to say:
*You realize the fundamental point.
You overcome the [unclear: "con"] of human life, free from entanglements.
In zazen, you are like a tiger.
A tiger ruling the waters.
A tiger roaming the mountains.
Freely sporting in the mountains.
In zazen, the Dharma emerges by itself, clearing away all hindrances and distractions.*
That's Dogen's description of zazen.
When we sit in zazen, we settle our body into the body of Buddha.
Our minds full of hindrances and distractions.
We actually become, as we sit, dignified Buddhas.
That's why when you walk into a zendo, you feel the unmistakable awesome feeling, to see all these dignified Buddhas sitting there.
We ourselves don't feel this probably or think this about ourselves, because that would be very stupid.
That would be a combination of arrogance and childishness all put together at the same time.
So it makes no sense for us to be thinking such things.
But that doesn't mean it's not so.
It is so, beyond our conceptualizations of it.
And because it really is so, we do feel it.
We feel it as the healing of our lives and the healing of the world.
And we are feeling this.
Maybe right now, while I'm saying this to you, it makes some sense to you.
And you know what I'm talking about.
But maybe a few weeks from now, if you were to hear this or read this, you would think, this is a little over the top.
This is very weird.
Religious cockeyed stuff, you know.
And you would be right.
From the point of view of everyday normal life, rational decision making, and ordinary coping, it's crazy to think that zazen is anything more than you trying your best to meditate.
But in fact, it is much more than that.
Like poetry, or any art, and like the inspired play of children, zazen and Buddhadharma itself is an act of the imagination.
A crazy and not crazy seeing beyond conventional reality through a more expansive and more heartfelt way of living.
We human beings have the capacity to feel our lives that way.
We have the capacity, but we have the necessity.
We have to be able to feel our lives that way.
If we don't, our lives are only this small [unclear: "crab"] life on this troubled planet with all these crazy people around.
If that's it, we can't go on that way.
We can't. [unclear: "But not when one of us can."] We need a bigger life.
Our hearts, our minds cry out for that.
So, let's keep working on this.
One more day maybe.
See what happens.
Thank you very much everybody for listening and for your practice.
